subject: prior on derived quantities (change of variables?)

messages.author: 8d1674b7b16af1b1
messages.subject: prior on derived quantities (change of variables?)
parts:
Some collaborators and I are working with a pretty big model, and we're running into some numerical problems with one of the parameters. The model includes a gamma-distributed GLM, which they parameterized in terms of a mean parameter and a rate (inverse scale) parameter:

    mean = exp(a + b * x);
    shape = mean * rate;
    y ~ gamma(shape, rate);

This part of the model is giving us some pretty serious numerical problems (e.g. up to 3% of the post-warm-up proposals get rejected because shape is 0, Inf, or NaN, and the remainder of the proposals are very slow when the mean isn't constant).

(I think that these problems are related to the fact that the full model includes a mixture of two very differently-distributed components, and that some of the observations are right-censored. As a result, a lot of observations [especially the imputed observations] fall way out in the right tail where gradients depend on the product of hugely negative conditional likelihoods and very tiny mixture weights.)

I was hoping to keep the shape parameter in a more reasonable range by putting a prior on it:

    shape ~ gamma(4, 1);

When I do this, I get warnings about non-linear transformations. I found the relevant sections of the Stan manual describing "Multivariate Changes of Variables", but I'm not confident enough in multivariate calculus to be sure how to proceed.

In terms of the equations listed in that section, I think my Y is `shape` and my Xs are `a`, `b`, and `rate`.  I know that I can invert the exponent with a logarithm, and I know how to calculate partial derivatives with respect to `a`, `b`, and `rate`, but I'm not totally clear on how to put it all together.  I looked for examples in the manual and in previous stan-users posts, but didn't find anything quite on-point (possibly because my search terms weren't good enough).

Assuming that putting a prior on the shape parameter is a reasonable thing to do, could someone point me toward an example of how I'd go about doing it for parameters of this form?

Thanks so much!

Dave

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: prior on gamma model
parts:
I think this is all fine, except that instead of
shape = mean*rate;
you should have:
rate = shape/mean;
I think this should work.  The idea is that "rate" is just an intermediate quantity; the parameters in the model are "shape", "a", and "b".
A

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] prior on gamma model
parts:
Do you just not understand how to add the Jacobian?
I would encourage you to consult a probability textbook
that discusses probability densities and changes of
variables, but I’ll summarize the basics here.

You want to put a prior on the derived quantity y = f(x).
Naively you can just substitute f(x) into the density,

p(y) -> p(f(x)),

this this does not define the correct density on x.  Instead
you need to include the Jacobian,

p(x) = p(f(x)) J(x)

where J(x) =  | dy / dx |.

Or in a Stan program,

parameters {
  real x;
  ...
}

transformed parameters {
  real y;
  y = f(x);
}

model {
  y ~ prior_dist(hyper_parameters);
  target += log(J(x));
  ...

}

On Jul 17, 2016, at 9:10 PM, David J. Harris <harr...@gmail.com> wrote:

I'd still be interested in help with the change of variables approach, since it seems like something that would be generally useful (e.g. http://andrewgelman.com/2013/07/19/prior-distributions-on-derived-quantities-rather-than-on-parameters-themselves/)

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] prior on derived quantities (change of variables?)
parts:
> On Jul 17, 2016, at 7:50 PM, David J. Harris <harr...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Some collaborators and I are working with a pretty big model, and we're running into some numerical problems with one of the parameters. The model includes a gamma-distributed GLM, which they parameterized in terms of a mean parameter and a rate (inverse scale) parameter:
>
> mean = exp(a + b * x);
> shape = mean * rate;
> y ~ gamma(shape, rate);

I'm guessing you want to declare Stan parameters (a, b, mean, rate)
and thus the program will define a density p(a, b, mean, rate).
Then you define shape as a transformed parameter as above.
shape = mean * rate;

That means your transform is

(a, b, mean, rate) |--> (a, b, mean, shape)


Then you want to define the model in terms of a density on
p(a, b, mean, shape).

a ~ ...;
b ~ ...;
mean ~ ...;
shape ~ ...;

Because the mapping from (a, b, mean) to (a, b, mean) is the identity,
the Jacobian's automaticaly lower triangular, so the Jacobian is
the product of the diagonal entries. The diagonal entries in the
Jacobian matrix are just

d.a / d.a = 1
d.b / d.b = 1
d.mean / d.mean = 1
d.shape / d.rate = mean

and the Jacobian determinant the product of the diagonal

|J| = abs(1 * 1 * 1 * mean)

with absolute value

|J| = abs(mean)

and the adjustment is then

log |J| = log(mean)

and the Jacobian can be expressed in Stan on the log scale is just

target += log(fabs(mean));

I think mean > 0 here, right, so you can drop the fabs function.

You'll want to double-check my work here.

- Bob
